records.our_prose: Radishes bolt, sending up a flower stalk, as temperatures rise and days lengthen in late spring and early summer. Bolting is driven by heat and long days together, not by a cold-then-warm vernalization sequence, so it is mainly a late-spring and summer problem. A bolting radish turns its energy to the flower stalk: the root stops sizing, turns woody and pithy, and the flavor goes sharp and hot. Because the crop is fast, the practical fix is timing, growing radishes in the cool windows on either side of summer, with heat-tolerant or slow-bolt varieties for the late-spring edge.

records.our_prose: Radishes are ready quickly and then go downhill fast, so check by size and pull them on time. The small round kinds are usually ready about 22 to 30 days after planting, when the radish is about an inch across. The tops of the radishes often poke up out of the soil, so you can see how big they are; pull one to check. Do not leave ready radishes sitting in the ground, especially in warm weather, or they turn hollow, woody, and very hot, and may crack. Pull round red radishes before they get bigger than about an inch, and white ones a little smaller. The long daikon kinds take longer, around 50 to 60 days; loosen the soil with a fork before pulling so the long root does not snap.

records.our_prose: The maggots (young larvae) of the cabbage maggot fly, a small gray fly. It spends the winter as pupae in the soil, and in spring the females lay lots of tiny white eggs at the base of cabbage-family plants. The eggs hatch in about a week and the maggots burrow into the roots for three to four weeks. It goes after the whole cabbage family, radishes, turnips, cabbage, broccoli, and kale, and is worst in cool, damp spring weather.

records.our_prose: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Radishes like it right around 6.0 to 6.8, slightly acidic, and they are not fussy as long as the soil is not packed hard. Do not stress over pH if your radishes are coming out fine, getting the soil loose and growing them fast matters more. If you want to know your number for certain, a cheap soil test from your local extension office will tell you, and let you know whether to add anything before planting.

records.our_prose: Radishes want loose, well-drained soil free of stones and clods, ideally a sandy loam or loam. Light, loose soil lets the root swell quickly and evenly, which is the whole game with radishes, because fast, unchecked growth is what keeps them mild and crisp. Loosen the bed at least 6 inches deep for small garden types, and a foot or more for long daikon and winter radishes; compacted or heavy clay soil gives small, misshapen, or forked roots. Work in well-rotted compost, but avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy tops and can cause the roots to branch or fork while the radish itself stays small. A slightly acidic to neutral pH around 6.0 to 6.8 suits them. If your soil is heavy, choose short round types or grow in a raised bed or deep container.

records.our_prose: Radishes like loose, crumbly soil, but they are much more forgiving than carrots. Loosen the soil about 6 inches deep for the small round kinds, and a foot or more for long daikon types, pulling out rocks and hard clumps so the radish can swell fast and evenly. Loose, sandy soil grows the cleanest radishes; heavy clay grows small, twisted ones, so mix in compost or use a raised bed. Do not add fresh manure or lots of high-nitrogen fertilizer before planting, since too much grows big leafy tops and can make the roots branch. Rake the top smooth so the little seeds sit snug against the soil, and aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8, which is slightly acidic.

records.our_prose: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, since radishes crack and split when soil swings from dry to wet and turn hot and woody under drought stress. Radish taproots reach for moisture but the feeder roots stay shallow, so the top few inches must not dry out. Aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, more in heat or sandy soil, keeping the bed evenly moist through the short, fast growing cycle.
